For some background, I currently live alone in New York City. My apartment building is wired for FiOS, and I have 25 Mbps up and down. I've been reading a lot about gigabit internet, and it seems exciting, but is it worth the upgrade if I'm living alone? I work 9-7 every day, so really only use my internet early in the morning and at night, and never regularly share my connection. I have a new 4K TV as well.

UPDATE: I've met in the middle and upgraded to 75 Mbps up and down on a no-term agreement. If I like what I see or feel the need to increase bandwidth further I can do so at will. Thanks for your help, Voat!!
How would I benefit from upgrading to gigabit internet service?

Do you personally need it, based on what you're describing probably not. When you start streaming 4k shows, though, you'll likely want more than your 25Mb connection. According to Netflix, you should have 25Mb connection for Ultra HD. Take this with a grain of salt, though, as I have a 1.5Mb connection and I stream SD fine with rarely any buffering. I also say you'll want more because Netflix will eat up most/all of your bandwidth with that Ultra HD show, so if you tend to do anything else while streaming then something's going to suffer.

Will you benefit from Google Fiber? Yes. Verizon will be forced to offer more bandwidth for the same/cheaper price. It's been several years since I last had FiOS, and around $60/month was getting me 75Mb/35Mb. For $70 anybody that has Google Fiber in their area can get 1Gb/1Gb. Need it or not, if I can get more for the same price I'll take it.

Way to bottom-line it. The "why" is simply that cord-cutting is the wave of the future. No, I haven't done it myself, but I honestly can't remember the last time I watched live network television, so it's probably something I should start considering, along with everyone else with the capacity to do so -- and bandwidth directly translates into capacity.

Also, as stated, why pay more for less?

Be careful about the Netflix 4k thing! I got all excited and signed up for it only to discover that it only works on an extremely limited number of devices because of DRM garbage (thanks studios). Unless it's changed in the last 6 months, you have to have a TV with a netflix app that supports 4k (I think the Sony 4k stand alone player may work too). IIRC they have some list of devices hiding somewhere on their site. Netflix has generally been amazing with respect to customer service, IMO this is the one place where they fall down. I wasted a whole day trying to figure out why my stream wasn't coming down in 4k. Then I finally discovered - No 4k streaming to PC allowed yet.
You definitely want a much faster connection than 25 for a 4K stream, considering how long it takes to download a 4K movie at 25mbps.
How much do you pay now? How much will the gigabit internet cost you?

It could be useful if the price isn't that different or you like the policy or customer service better on the other plan, or if you want to stick it to Verizon for their multiple attempts to drastically increase the price of online services you use. You'd have much faster file transfers when you want to download something outright instead of streaming it.

Supposing you want to fully download a 4K movie that's 160GB or so... Do you want to do that at 3 MB/sec or 119MB/sec? 15 hours or 23 minutes?

Three reasons off the top of my head.

First, streaming UHD. Second, downloading large files (high quality video with lossless audio is a big one, also major game releases). Third, gaming on servers in the EU or Asia.

Setting aside video streaming, there are some less obvious benefits to something like gigabit ethernet service, especially from a company other than Time Warner or Comcast.

What I'd say first is that once the technology comes, engineers will find ways of using it. Before widespread broadband, we actually did have "streaming video" online; at about 100x100 pixels in a tiny little sad window. It sucked. We had voice/video conferencing, and it too was terrible, with garbled voices and a new frame every few seconds. Along came broadband and now we have 1080p streaming and 60fms video conferencing.

Now, think of what currently sucks. Virtual Reality is something they've been talking about since the 80s/90s, and it continues to suck, but the Oculus Rift has almost gotten hardware right. What about content? Streaming all the information a computer needs to render an Oculus Rift-type world is well outside of 25Mbps, but at a gigabit connection speed, it seems feasible that you could have a high-fidelity virtual world. Think of Second Life, but with a 3d headset, and rendering quality of at least Toy Story 1. It's on the horizon, technology-wise, but it'll require significantly more bandwidth than we currently have.

Though perhaps more so, we don't know yet what engineers and creative people will do with more bandwidth. They don't have it, but when they do, it's like giving the art world another color to paint with: you don't know what will come, but it'll be amazing.

For VOAT users, here's a plus: One obvious benefit is that a vast expansion of bandwidth in the consumer home -- yours and others -- would really facilitate technologies meant to defeat Internet censorship. Tor, for example, is very bandwidth intensive, and with the extra bandwidth, you could participate at some level in supporting Tor. You could also help use peer-to-peer technology, like bittorrent or technologies that bypass DNS, to defeat censorship.

Finally, if you get bandwidth from the likes of Google Fiber, is that there's going to be less "traffic shaping." Almost no one with 25Mbps actually gets 25Mbps for any sustained period of time, in part because companies like Comcast are extorting tier 1 networks for peering, thus slowing down traffic regardless of your personal uplink to Comcast. Google Fiber has yet to engage in those, well, shenanigans. Municipal broadband companies also haven't been a problem.

For now, I've upgraded to 75Mbps up and down. I'm uber excited for VR, but I'm unsatisfied with current consumer offerings. I think this is a happy medium, and I've signed a no-term agreement so I can upgrade at-will if I like the change in my internet. Thanks for your detailed response!
